And there was a particular vogue for "transcriptions" or "variations" pieces in which hymn tunes or other familiar melodies were embedded in elaborate concert-hall treatment; one such of the decoration devices, and other evidences of manual dexterity. Popular ones encountered by this quest include "Rock of Ages," "Sweetly Rest," "Rock Beside the Sea," "Death Is Only a Dream," "Bonnie Doon," Gustav Lang's "Flower Song," and Leybach's "Fifth Nocturne."

On one night of exhibition week there was a "levee" for the young people after the program. Mr. Sam McKee of Bells, Texas, adds the information, "we just marched to the music and then went in a big circle—something like the Virginia Reel. The county judges of Fannin, Hunt, and Grayson were the county judges of Fannin, Hunt, and Grayson were the county judges of Fannin, Hunt, and Grayson.

And, for San Jacinto Day we had a 'hat' or negative side.

The Memorable Debate with Grayson College.—One of the most outstanding events in the memories of many ex-students was the debate on the 27th Anniversary of the Sam Houston and Union Literary Societies of Grayson College, which took place in the early 1890's (before or after 1891) at Whitewright, Texas, between the Platonian Society of Savoy College and the literary societies of Grayson College (at McKinney), which took place in the early 1890's. The debate subject was, "Resolved that the Negro should be colonized." The Savoy boys took the affirmative side, argued by Messrs. J. B. Thompson and J. C. Watson and G. W. Truett.
